answers.java_tx_design: I redesigned the transaction boundary on our wallet-ledger-service about three years in. Originally a ride completion wrapped the fare split, driver credit, and promo deduction in one transaction against a table doing roughly 1,200 writes per second at peak, and we were seeing lock waits climb past 300ms during surge pricing windows. I split it into a fast, single-row balance update inside the original transaction, with the fare-split detail and promo deduction written asynchronously via an outbox pattern and a Kafka consumer. Lock wait dropped to under 20ms at the same peak load. The failure that taught me this: an early version of the outbox consumer wasn't idempotent, and a consumer restart during a deploy double-applied about 600 promo deductions before we caught it in the next morning's reconciliation.
answers.java_ops: We had recurring GC pauses on driver-payout-service — full stop-the-world pauses of 800ms to 1.2 seconds every few minutes under load, enough to trip our p99 latency SLO. I pulled GC logs and found we were on CMS with a heap sized for a much smaller instance after a resize. Switched to G1GC, tuned the heap to 6GB with a 200ms pause target, and pauses dropped to under 100ms. Separately, we had a connection pool exhaustion incident where a slow downstream fraud-check call was holding HikariCP connections for 8+ seconds; I added a 2-second timeout on that call and doubled the pool from 15 to 30, which fixed it within the same deploy.
answers.rust_readiness: No production Rust yet. I've been through the official book and built a small toy project — a CLI that replays our wallet transaction logs and recomputes balances, mostly to get a feel for ownership without the pressure of a real deadline. That took about six weekends. For something real, I wouldn't try to port a whole service; I'd pick a narrow, well-understood piece — something like the fee calculation logic, which is pure computation with no I/O — run it side-by-side with the Java version, diff the outputs, and only cut over once they matched for a couple of weeks under real traffic. A full rewrite of anything stateful feels like the wrong way to spend the risk budget.
answers.rust_boundary: If I were moving part of the ledger write path to Rust, I'd start with the balance-computation step, not the persistence layer — keep Postgres writes in Java and have Rust own just the arithmetic and validation, called over a narrow gRPC boundary. Before migrating I'd want p99 latency and allocation rate on the current Java path as a baseline, plus a shadow run where the Rust service computes the same result without being trusted, so I can diff its output against Java's for real traffic before switching anything over. I did something similar carving a fraud-scoring module out of our monolith into its own Java service a few years back — the numbers-first, dual-run approach is the same instinct, just a different language this time.
answers.money_correctness: wallet-ledger-service dedupes ride-completion events using an idempotency key of ride ID plus event type, enforced with a unique constraint in Postgres, and every payout callback carries the same key on retry. It broke once: a downstream retry from our payment processor came back with a slightly different key format after a deploy on their end changed how they encoded ride IDs, so our uniqueness check didn't catch it, and about 340 rides got double-credited to driver balances over a five-hour window, roughly $4,100 total. I caught it from an anomaly in our daily balance-drift report the next morning. We corrected it with new offsetting ledger entries, not edits to the originals, and added a secondary check that also compares payout amount and timestamp proximity, not just the key.
answers.incident_response: That double-credit incident: I got the alert at 7:40am from the drift report, confirmed the scope by 8:15 — 340 rides, five-hour window — and had the offsetting entries running by 9:30, fully corrected by 11. I told my manager and the payments lead as soon as I confirmed it was real, before I had the fix, not after. The postmortem's main action item was the key-format validation I mentioned, which we shipped within the week, plus an alert on the drift report threshold dropping from daily to hourly. Six months later it hasn't recurred, and the hourly alert did catch a smaller, unrelated blip early once.
answers.process_skipping: During that incident I skipped our normal two-reviewer rule for the offsetting-entry script — I posted it in the incident channel, got one quick approval from my manager instead of two, and we'd all agreed on that lower bar beforehand as our incident-response standard, not something I decided alone in the moment. Once things were stable I opened a proper PR for the permanent validation fix and it went through full review like anything else. I've never skipped procedure outside an actual declared incident — if something's not literally on fire, it goes through the normal process.
answers.hiding_and_oncall: The double-credit incident is also the mistake-sharing example — I told people the moment I confirmed it, not after I'd already fixed it quietly. On-call: I've done it for about six years now, roughly one week in six, and I still take it, seniority or not — I think that's part of owning what you build. I also mentor two junior engineers on the team, weekly pairing sessions, mostly around debugging production issues and reading incident timelines, since that's the skill that took me longest to build myself.
answers.evidence_decision: I disagreed with a plan to move driver payouts to a nightly batch instead of near-real-time, for cost reasons. I pulled three months of support ticket data showing same-day payout was our top driver-satisfaction driver in exit surveys, and modeled the actual infra cost difference, which was smaller than the initial estimate. The team decided to keep near-real-time payouts but batch just the reporting side, a middle option I hadn't proposed. I built that instead of pushing my original idea further once the decision was made.
answers.own_contribution: On the fraud-scoring carve-out I mentioned earlier: identifying which parts were pure computation versus stateful was my analysis, and the dual-run comparison approach was mine; the decision on the final cutover date was made jointly with the fraud team once we'd both signed off on two weeks of matching output. On the GC tuning, the diagnosis and the G1GC switch were mine alone; the decision to also resize the instance type afterward involved our infra team's input on cost.
answers.java_recovery: Scoping the double-credit incident: I wrote a query joining ride completions against ledger entries grouped by ride ID, counting entries where the sum didn't match the expected single credit, which surfaced the 340 affected rides across that five-hour window. I fixed it with new offsetting entries dated at correction time, not by touching the originals, then reran our nightly balance-reconciliation job against the affected driver IDs to confirm every one landed at zero net difference before closing the incident.
answers.java_perf_change: I cut p99 latency on the ride-completion endpoint from 640ms to 180ms by profiling with async-profiler and finding we were doing a synchronous fraud-score lookup inline that averaged 400ms. Moved it to run in parallel with the ledger write instead of before it, since the two don't actually depend on each other. First attempt was just adding a cache in front of the fraud-score call, but scores go stale within seconds for a new driver, so that caused a handful of wrong approvals in testing before I reverted it and did the parallelization instead.
answers.rust_hands_on: In that toy log-replay CLI, I got stuck trying to hold a mutable reference to my in-memory balance map while iterating over the same map to validate entries — classic borrow-checker fight. I ended up collecting the validation results into a separate Vec first, then applying updates in a second pass instead of trying to do both in one loop. Not elegant, but it's the point where ownership rules actually clicked for me instead of just being something I'd read about.
answers.rust_when_not: I wouldn't move the fee-calculation rules engine — it changes almost weekly as pricing experiments roll out, and none of us are fast enough in Rust yet to iterate at that speed. I have held back a rewrite before, actually: I wanted to rebuild our promo-eligibility service from scratch a couple years ago because the code was messy, but a teammate pointed out it had zero incidents in over a year, so we just refactored the worst function in place instead and left the rest alone.
answers.reconciliation_mismatch: Separate incident: our daily settlement once showed a $1,850 gap. Traced it to a batch of ride cancellations with partial refunds that landed after our nightly reconciliation cutoff but got backdated to the prior day by the payment processor's clock, which ran a few minutes ahead of ours. Took about three hours to find using transaction timestamps against processor timestamps side by side. We fixed it by reconciling on processor-reported time instead of our received time, and corrected the affected day with a new entry rather than moving anything retroactively.
answers.prod_data_verification: When I needed to verify the key-format fix actually caught the duplicate case, I didn't test it against real driver balances — I replayed the exact failing event from the incident against a staging database seeded with masked production-shaped data, and confirmed the new check rejected it. For a separate case where staging genuinely couldn't reproduce a race condition, I ran a read-only shadow comparison in production — the new code path computed a result but nothing was written — announced it in the incident channel first and limited it to a two-hour window.
